title: The Secretary of Imprecision
text:
O ver the past several days , as anxious Americans watched software systems crash, air traffic halt, and banking services glitch—wondering each time whether the country was falling victim to a catastrophic cyberattack—it has been Markwayne Mullin’s job to reassure them. Delivering clear and careful explanations, unfortunately, is not his forte.

 The Department of Homeland Security secretary’s speaking style is more free-associative. Mullin first rose to prominence by building his family’s plumbing business into a home-services giant in northeast Oklahoma. His sentences still tend to travel like a drain line, making loops and turns en route to an unseen destination. He doesn’t seem to work from talking points.

 Mullin parlayed this folksy manner and Everyman relatability into a successful bid for Congress in 2012. He wore a cowboy hat around Washington, D.C., and became one of President Trump’s fiercest allies on Capitol Hill. When Trump picked him to replace Kristi Noem at DHS earlier this year, he carried a reputation as the martial artist of MAGA politics. This made Mullin a somewhat unusual choice for a job that, until Trump’s second term, had typically been held by more buttoned-up figures who choose their words carefully, especially during moments of crisis.

 Soon after the FAA lifted its hours-long ground stop on Friday evening, Mullin appeared alongside Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and announced that the problem was likely caused by the FAA’s own upgrades. This put the onus on Duffy, who stared at the floor and shook his head. The two have not appeared at briefings together since. Three nights later, after thousands of Chase Bank customers were unable to access their accounts and other financial institutions’ clients reported problems with digital payments, Mullin appeared on Sean Hannity’s Fox News show and described a conversation that he’d had a few hours earlier with “one guy that’s very smart with tech” (but not, Mullin made clear, Elon Musk) who had claimed that AI was indirectly causing the outages. “As it starts self-fixing itself it’s like doing a change order on a house,” Mullin said, using a home-improvement analogy.

 It wasn’t clear whether this assessment was coming from cybersecurity experts—particularly those at the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, which is under Mullin’s command at DHS. Mullin said with “98 percent certainty” that the outages were not cyberattacks. By Tuesday, Mullin was able to add that last 2 percent, saying during a CNBC interview: “I can tell you with complete certainty that we are not under attack.” He gave no indication of how he’d arrived at that view. (Three minutes later, his certainty regressed to 98 percent.)

 One frustrated senior DHS official who didn’t want to be identified bad-mouthing the boss told me that Mullin “gives the perception that he’s winging it,” adding that “he’s giving Biden a run for his money with the frequency of gaffes.”

 [ Read: The secretary of homeland ] 

 Late-night comedians are now mocking him—along with right-wing commentators. The podcaster Megyn Kelly declared that “he seems like an idiot.” Steve Bannon, a longtime adviser to the president, said on his War Room show that he is “not so sure it’s helpful to keep putting Markwayne Mullin on shows like Sean Hannity or even have him go on CNBC.” Mullin followed those wobbly appearances with testimony before the House Homeland Security Committee yesterday—and used nearly his entire opening statement to angrily justify flying on a government jet to see a college-football game in Louisiana less than 24 hours after the FAA ground stop had been lifted, as thousands of travelers remained stranded. “I wanted to be a good uncle and take my little niece, who has never been to an LSU game, and she’s a huge LSU fan, to a game,” he said.

 By then, the White House had already seemingly relieved Mullin from his role as the designated explainer of the mysterious outages, replacing him with Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton, who brings a more lawyerly bearing. “Good move by the White House,” former Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt wrote on X as Clayton took the lead on Fox News.

 In a statement, DHS told me that “Mullin surrounds himself with a variety of experts” from across the department’s 22 agencies and components. “Secretary Mullin employs a management style that empowers his agency heads, his staff, and every individual,” the statement said, citing his track record on deportations, border security, and drug seizures. “The results speak for themselves.”

 D HS secretaries have to be conversant on a range of topics, such as airline travel, cybersecurity , and operations of the U.S. Secret Service. What has usually tripped up Mullin in his new role, especially among right-wing critics, has been his imprecise statements about immigration enforcement. Handling immigration might be the most politically charged part of his job, and partisans on all sides are looking for signifiers in every statement and utterance.

 During his confirmation hearing, Mullin told lawmakers that he wanted to turn down the visibility and temperature of Trump’s mass-deportation campaign, relaying the direction he had received from the White House following the killing of two U.S. citizens during an ICE crackdown in Minneapolis. Immigration arrests and deportations have reached record highs in recent months, but some of the president’s most ardent supporters—among them, loyalists to Noem —have retained their skepticism of Mullin.

 During his years in Congress, Mullin was one of the biggest supporters of Trump’s border wall, but he also spoke favorably of hardworking immigrants who stay out of trouble. Some of the gaffes and misstatements that Mullin has made over the past several weeks have fanned claims from hard-liners that he’s not as committed to mass deportations as Noem’s team. After Democrats’ historic midterm wins, Mullin said that Congress could work on immigration reform “where we can look at DACA and figure out a way that these individuals can become maybe legal permanent citizens or something like this.” There is no such thing as “legal permanent citizens” in U.S. immigration law, and Mullin appeared to conflate legal permanent residency with U.S. citizenship. But it was Mullin’s mention of President Obama’s Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals program that triggered the greatest outrage on the right. Mullin said that some DACA recipients “may not even speak English or never even lived in their country,” apparently intending to say that such people spoke only English.

 Trump and others have insisted that the administration would not support “amnesty,” the proposals for legal pathways that hard-liners deplore, but that was the word Mullin used last week during an interview with Fox News when he meant to say “asylum,” the immigration process for border crossers who claim to be fleeing persecution in their home country. “If they want to talk about making people that enter this country here illegally legal, that’s a nonstarter,” Mullin told Laura Ingraham. “If they want to talk about how do we reform amnesty and how the port of entries work,” Mullin said before Ingraham cut in.

 Mullin has referred to gang members as “serious affiliated drug bangers” and used the term collateral criminals instead of collateral arrests —ICE’s term for people who were not the intended target of immigration raids but were swept up as well, regardless of whether they have criminal records. Mullin has also gotten in trouble for appearing to speak out of turn. After an ICE officer in Maine fatally shot a Colombian delivery driver on July 13 while his family was nearby, Mullin gave an order to suspend nonessential traffic stops. Immigration hard-liners protested to Trump, saying that the move made the administration look weak, and the next day, Trump reversed the order .

 T here’s been no indication that Trump is preparing to fire Mullin, despite calls on the right for his replacement. Getting another secretary nominated and confirmed in the Senate will become much more difficult after Democrats take control in January. Mullin has never committed the cardinal sin of Trumpism: disloyalty. And Trump himself misstates immigration law and facts almost every time he discusses the topic, layering his speeches with made-up numbers (“25 million people came in illegally”), unsubstantiated claims (immigrants sent from “insane asylums”), and flagrant lies (“they’re eating the dogs, the people that came in; they’re eating the cats”).

 Trump told 60 Minutes after the midterms that his immigration crackdown had been “too tough” and that he is open to working with Democrats. He then proceeded to name Stephen Miller, the driving force behind his mass-deportation campaign, as White House chief of staff. Representative Hakeem Jeffries, the Democratic nominee for speaker of the House, has said that he won’t work with Miller, calling him a “stone-cold racist.”

 Miller’s promotion may help Mullin keep his job a bit longer. The most hawkish voices in the MAGA movement want Trump to double down on mass deportations, and Mullin has demonstrated that he’s more than willing to continue on that course if the White House directs him to do so—even if he talks out of turn or flubs his interviews.
